name: recon
label: Reconnaissance

tools.name: nmap
tools.use: Port, service and version scan, plus the NSE script library. The core active recon tool once you have a live host.
tools.args: -sV fingerprints services and versions, -sS runs a SYN scan (uses NET_RAW, falls back to a connect scan if unavailable), -p PORTS limits the range, --script vuln runs the cheap known-issue checks, -oN FILE writes a report. Ends with the target host or CIDR.

tools.name: masscan
tools.use: Sweep a wide port or address range fast, then hand the open ports to nmap for detail.
tools.args: A target range and -p PORTS, with --rate PPS to cap the packet rate. -oL FILE writes the open ports. Uses NET_RAW.

tools.name: subfinder
tools.use: Passive subdomain enumeration from many sources at once.
tools.args: -d DOMAIN for the target, -silent prints one host per line with no banner, -all uses every source, -o FILE writes them.

tools.name: amass
tools.use: OWASP subdomain and infrastructure OSINT — the passive mode stays off the target.
tools.args: The `enum` subcommand, then -passive to stay off the target (or -active to resolve), -d DOMAIN, -o FILE for output.

tools.name: dnsx
tools.use: Bulk DNS: resolve a host list, brute a wordlist, pull A/AAAA/CNAME/MX/TXT records, drop wildcards.
tools.args: -l HOSTS.txt (or -d DOMAIN -w WORDLIST to brute), with record flags -a/-aaaa/-cname/-mx/-txt, -resp to show the answer and -silent for one line each.

tools.name: httpx
tools.use: Probe a host list for live HTTP — status, title, server, detected tech, TLS — one line each. The first move after subdomain enum.
tools.args: -l HOSTS.txt (or -u URL) with -sc for status, -title, -server, -tech-detect, -silent, and -o FILE to write the live ones.

tools.name: katana
tools.use: Crawl a site for endpoints, forms and parameters — the map a deeper test starts from. No JavaScript engine, so it will not reach client-rendered routes.
tools.args: -u URL to crawl, -d N sets depth, -jc follows JavaScript-derived endpoints from static analysis, -o FILE writes the URLs found.

tools.name: tlsx
tools.use: Grab TLS certificate data — subject, SANs, issuer, expiry — across many hosts.
tools.args: -l HOSTS.txt (or -u HOST:PORT) with -san, -cn for names, -expired for expiry, -silent for one line each.

tools.name: gau
tools.use: getallurls — pull known URLs for a domain from Wayback, Common Crawl and others (OSINT).
tools.args: One or more domains as plain arguments. --subs includes subdomains, --threads N parallelises, --o FILE writes them.

tools.name: waybackurls
tools.use: List every path the Wayback Machine has seen for a host — a cheap map of the surface.
tools.args: A domain as the argument, or a list of domains on stdin. Prints one URL per line to redirect into a file.

tools.name: whois
tools.use: Domain and netblock registration OSINT — registrar, dates, name servers, org.
tools.args: A domain or IP address.

tools.name: dig
tools.use: Direct DNS queries. `host` and `nslookup` are here too for the same job.
tools.args: A name, optionally a record type (A, AAAA, MX, TXT, NS, CNAME) and @resolver. +short trims to the answer.

tools.name: sslscan
tools.use: Enumerate a host's TLS versions, ciphers and certificate — the quick TLS posture check.
tools.args: A host, or host:port. --no-failed hides rejected ciphers, --xml=FILE writes a report.

tools.name: rg
tools.use: Search inside files you already saved to the workspace.
tools.args: A pattern and a path, relative to the workspace. -n prints line numbers, -i ignores case.

tools.name: jq
tools.use: Filter or reshape JSON, usually from curl or a scanner's -json output.
tools.args: A jq filter, then a file — or nothing after it to read stdin.

tools.name: anew
tools.use: Append only new lines to a file — the way to dedupe a growing host or URL list across runs.
tools.args: The file to append to, reading candidate lines on stdin; prints only the lines that were new.

tools.name: gf
tools.use: Grep with named patterns (gf ssrf, gf xss, gf sqli) to pull interesting URLs out of a crawl.
tools.args: A pattern name — ssrf, xss, sqli, redirect and the like — reading URLs on stdin.

tools.name: curl
tools.use: Call an API or fetch raw HTTP, when you want the bytes rather than a rendered page.
tools.args: -sSL and a URL for a plain GET; -i includes response headers, -X METHOD, -H 'Header: v' and -d BODY shape a request. Use fetch for anything you intend to read as text.

tools.name: wget
tools.use: Download a file or mirror a small path to the workspace.
tools.args: A URL. -O FILE names the output, -q silences progress, -r -np -l N mirrors a small subtree.

tools.name: openssl
tools.use: Inspect a site's TLS certificate — issuer, subject, the names it covers and when it expires — and do the everyday crypto odd jobs: hashes, base64, random bytes.
tools.args: s_client -connect HOST:443 -servername HOST </dev/null 2>/dev/null | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName reads a live certificate. Local forms take no network: dgst -sha256 FILE, base64 -d, rand -hex 16.

tools.name: python3
tools.use: Run Python, for anything the other commands cannot express — glue between the scanners, or a custom request.
tools.args: -c and a program, or a script path. requests is installed.

notes: This box reaches the target and the OSINT sources directly, so treat that traffic as attributable to this machine, and only scan hosts you are permitted to. Work in stages and write each to a file — enumerate subdomains (subfinder, amass), resolve them (dnsx), find live HTTP (httpx), scan ports and services (nmap, masscan), crawl for endpoints (katana, gau, waybackurls), gather OSINT (whois), audit TLS (sslscan, tlsx) — and dedupe growing lists with `anew` rather than holding them in context. There is no browser and no JavaScript engine, so `katana` will not reach client-rendered routes. NET_RAW is granted so `nmap -sS` can raw-scan; it falls back to a connect scan on its own if unavailable. Paths are the same ones the file tools use: write `recon/hosts.txt`, not an absolute path. Output too large to return inline is kept under /run/ghost-runs/ — reach it with a shell command, not the file tools.
